subject: Archaeology
subcategory: Lost Cities of the Ancient World
title: Chan Chan: The Largest Adobe City
description: A fast breakdown of Chan Chan: The Largest Adobe City for builders.

hook.text: The largest mud-brick city ever built is slowly dissolving in the rain on Peru's northern coast.

buildup.text: Chan Chan was the capital of the Chimú Empire, covering eight square miles and housing 60,000 people by 1400 CE.

discovery.text: Its walls are covered in intricate friezes of fish, birds, and waves — all carved into dried mud.

twist.text: The Inca conquered the Chimú in 1470 by diverting their water supply. No battle was needed — just thirst.

climax.text: El Niño rains are eroding the city faster each decade. Climate change may destroy what the Inca could not.

punchline.text: An empire fell to thirst. Its capital is falling to rain.

quiz.question: How did the Inca conquer the Chimú at Chan Chan?
options: They laid siege for three years until food ran out
They diverted the city's water supply, defeating them with thirst
They used superior bronze weapons to overwhelm mud-brick walls

details.summary: Chan Chan in Peru was the capital of the Chimú Empire and the largest adobe city ever built, covering about 20 square kilometers. Its nine royal compounds contained ornate wall friezes, walk-in wells, and burial platforms. El Niño rains and the Inca conquest led to its decline after 1470 CE.
details.whyItMatters: Chan Chan demonstrates that monumental architecture does not require stone. Mudbrick construction created a vast royal capital that housed up to 60,000 people — but its adobe material makes it extremely vulnerable to climate-driven erosion.
takeaways: The largest adobe city ever built, covering 20 square kilometers
Capital of the Chimú Empire housing up to 60,000 people
El Niño rains threaten the adobe structures with erosion and collapse

faq.question: Why is Chan Chan considered endangered?
faq.answer: Adobe dissolves in rain, and El Niño events bring heavy rainfall to the normally arid coast. Each El Niño cycle damages exposed walls. Rising groundwater from modern irrigation also undermines foundations. UNESCO lists Chan Chan as endangered World Heritage due to these ongoing threats.

faq.question: How was Chimú society organized at Chan Chan?
faq.answer: Each of nine royal compounds was built for a specific ruler and sealed after his death. The ruler was buried with attendants and goods inside. Commoners lived in surrounding neighborhoods. The compounds' increasing size suggests the empire grew wealthier over successive reigns.
